public_rationale: On March 14, 2023, OpenAI acknowledged that GPT-4 still hallucinated facts and made reasoning errors [e1]. The April 14 API-Bank paper reported a 40% success rate for GPT-3.5-Turbo on tasks requiring API retrieval, alongside other tool-use failures [e2]. The study revised August 1 found substantial task-dependent changes between March and June 2023 versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, including improvements and regressions [e3]. These findings support the observation that the listed reliability problems remained unresolved in the systems studied [e1, e2, e3]. OpenAI's July 20 documentation offered stable pinned versions, limiting the engineering implications of changes across releases [e4].
limitations: API-Bank does not directly evaluate Wolfram Alpha or every model available in August 2023.
The March–June comparison does not establish changes within an unchanged, pinned model or deterioration on every task.
The evidence does not establish that every generative model or engineering integration was unreliable or unsuitable.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Generative AI has many serious unsolved core problems, including hallucination, unreliable tool use, and month-to-month instability.

statement.excerpt: We have not one, but many, serious, unsolved problems at the core of generative AI — ranging from their tendency to confabulate (hallucinate) false information, to their inability to reliably interface with external tools like Wolfram Alpha, to the instability from month to month (which makes them poor candidates for engineering use in larger systems).
statement.document_title: What if Generative AI turned out to be a Dud?

from_speaker: inability to reliably interface with external tools like Wolfram Alpha
our_interpretation: The plain reading is that important reliability problems persisted in contemporary general-purpose language models, not that every model failed every task.

The present-tense observation concerns systems available before publication. With no common reporting cycle, the observation window is calendar 2023 through August 13; this period convention is an evaluator choice.
Reliability requires more than successful demonstrations. Repeated factual errors, failed tool interactions, and material changes between model versions qualify.
The engineering parenthesis is treated as an implication of those problems, not a claim that no useful integration was possible.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary documentation and evaluations establish persistent factual errors, material tool-use failures, and behavior changes between monthly versions of leading systems.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporary evaluations establish that the listed problems had been reliably resolved. Successful individual demonstrations alone do not establish this.

evidence.explanation: OpenAI explicitly acknowledged continuing factual errors in its released model. The same section reports improvements, so persistence should not be confused with lack of progress.

The benchmark documents substantial failures in retrieving and using external APIs. This supports the general tool-reliability concern, but is not a Wolfram Alpha evaluation or a test of every August model.

evidence.explanation: The study found task-dependent changes between March and June versions, including improvements and regressions. It establishes version-dependent behavior, not universal deterioration or drift within an unchanged model.

evidence.locator: July 20, 2023 update, paragraph about evaluation metrics and version pinning
evidence.explanation: OpenAI offered stable pinned versions while acknowledging regressions across upgrades. This limits the implication that every engineering integration necessarily faced uncontrolled monthly changes.
